Opening the United States Regions Gallery
🎬
Teacher recording notes: Greet students warmly. Say: "Welcome, United States Region Curators! Today we open the United States Regions Gallery — five alcoves, each waiting for one region." Read the Curator's Question: "How do geographers divide the United States into regions, and what makes each region its own place?" Briefly introduce the five region names on the map. Spotlight courtesy: we talk about every region — even the ones we've never visited — with curiosity and respect. Under 2 minutes.
🏛️ Virtue Spotlight: Courtesy
When we study regions, we study real places where real people live. Courtesy means we talk about every region, the ones we've been to and the ones we haven't, with the same respect and curiosity. No region is "boring" or "better." People also see places in different ways. A visitor might call a desert empty. Someone who lives there knows it is full of plants, animals, and neighbors. Every alcove in this gallery deserves equal attention.

🔍 TEACHING · EXPLORE
The Five Regions of the United States
🎬
Teacher recording notes: Point to a U.S. map and walk through each region by name and location: Northeast (upper right, Atlantic coast), Southeast (lower right, Gulf + Atlantic), Midwest (central interior heartland), Southwest (desert, canyons, Rio Grande), West (Pacific coast + Rockies). Explain what geographers use to group states into regions: shared land, climate, resources, and human patterns. Share one standout fact for each region. Remind students that courtesy means we explore every region with the same curiosity. 3–5 minutes.
1
The United States Regions Gallery Opens
📖
What Is a Region?
Five alcoves, one country

Geographers are people who study the earth and its places. They group states into a region when the states share the same land, climate (the usual weather), resources, or ways of life. Many maps divide the United States into five regions: Northeast, Southeast, Midwest, Southwest, and West.

🏙️ Northeast
Upper-right corner, along the Atlantic Ocean. Some of the oldest cities in the country, lobster and fishing boats, forests, and the Appalachian Mountains.States: Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Maryland.
🌴 Southeast
Lower-right corner, on the Atlantic Ocean and the Gulf of Mexico. Warm weather, the Everglades, cotton and orange farms, and the southern Appalachian Mountains.States: Florida, Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Arkansas, Tennessee, Kentucky, West Virginia, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina.
🌽 Midwest
The middle of the country. Flat plains, part of the Great Plains, the Great Lakes, and the Mississippi River. So many corn and wheat farms that people call it the "Breadbasket of America."States: Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa, Missouri, North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Kansas.
🌵 Southwest
Lower middle, next to Mexico. Dry, sunny deserts, canyons like the Grand Canyon, the Rio Grande, oil wells, and cattle ranches.States: Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico, Arizona.
🏔️ West
Left side, along the Pacific Ocean. The Rocky Mountains and many different climates, from rainforests in Washington to deserts in Nevada. Alaska and Hawaii are in the West too.States: Washington, Oregon, California, Nevada, Idaho, Montana, Wyoming, Utah, Colorado, Alaska, Hawaii.
🦸

Heroes in Every Region: Heroes come from every region. Rosa Parks stood up for fair treatment in Alabama, in the Southeast. Barack Obama worked in Illinois, in the Midwest, before he became the 44th President of the United States. People from many backgrounds shaped every region. Spanish settlers gave many Southwest cities their names, like San Antonio and Santa Fe. As you study each region, look for the people who made it proud.

⏳

Then & Now: Long ago, travelers crossing the country by wagon watched the land change: flat, grassy plains, then tall, rocky mountains, then dry deserts. Today we can fly across the country in a few hours, but the land is still different from place to place. That is why geographers still study regions.

🔎 Discovery Fact
The United States has 50 states. Many maps group them into five regions. Some maps use four regions instead, so region lines can be drawn a little differently.
🏷️ Exhibit Label

Many maps divide the United States into five regions: Northeast, Southeast, Midwest, Southwest, and West. Each region has its own land, climate, resources, and ways of life. Studying regions helps us understand how the United States is both one country and many different places.

🦉
🧭 Opti says…
Did you know different maps sometimes group states differently? Texas is usually in the Southwest, but some maps put it in a region called the South. Region lines are drawn by people, so they can be drawn a little differently.

Five regions named, five alcove signs in place. Let's check what you remember before you write your gallery notes.

Quick Self-Check
🧠

Not graded. Just for you! Answer these three questions before writing your evidence responses.

1. What do geographers use to group states into regions?
AOnly the names of rivers and mountains
BWhich states are the biggest
CThe land, climate, resources, and ways of life the states share
Yes! Geographers group states that share the same land, climate, resources, and ways of life, like the sheets on the Light Table.
Think about the four sheets: land, weather, resources, and how people live. Geographers look for what the states share.
2. Which region has the Great Lakes, flat plains, and huge corn and wheat farms?
ANortheast
BMidwest
CSouthwest
Yes! The Midwest's flat plains are perfect for farming. People call it the "Breadbasket of America." The Great Lakes are there too!
The Northeast has old cities and rocky coasts. The Southwest has deserts and canyons. Which region sits around the Great Lakes?
3. Into how many regions do many maps divide the United States?
AFive
BThree
CEight
Yes! Northeast, Southeast, Midwest, Southwest, and West: five alcoves, five regions.
Count the alcoves in the Regions Gallery. One alcove holds one region.
